idiom_name: private var members of the smallest owning class; method-local state; immutable case-class values passed down to stateless children
implementation_notes: Scala places state with the same class-local rule as other object languages: declare it as a private var in the smallest class that uses it (or in a small per-screen state holder), and keep transient values as locals. Because idiomatic Scala prefers immutability, the most common realization is stronger than a private cell: the owner holds the state and passes immutable case-class values down to children that stay stateless, so the mutable cell exists in exactly one place and the rest of the tree cannot observe it - colocation plus immutability. The replacement for the classic structure is that single owner: a top-level object with mutable members is a process-wide singleton (Scala's app-level store), and shared mutable state between components belongs in their closest common owner, guarded explicitly if it is touched concurrently.
pitfalls: Members of a top-level object are process-wide singletons; an AppState object that everything imports is the Scala shape of a global store and is easy to grow accidentally.
A var in a shared instance is not thread-safe by itself; concurrent access needs synchronization or an atomic/concurrent structure owned by the same object.
Closures and partial functions defined inside the class capture this, so listeners registered on long-lived actors or dispatchers keep the owner (and its state) alive.
